tier_reason: The numbers come from the project's own arXiv preprint (Ant Digital Technologies authors, not peer reviewed; resources/DTVM_paper.pdf, April 2025), which states the CPU (Xeon Platinum 8369B) but not the DTVM build type or run flags. The reproduction package benchmarks/paper ships cases and reconstructed scripts but no result data or the paper's timing script; its runtimes/dtvm/BUILD.md says the paper-era run CLI was 'inferred from xlsx', and docs/XLSX_FORMAT.md says the archived table's semantics (compile vs total, ms vs s) are unconfirmed. Flags absent from public sources and first-party authorship cap this at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper (arXiv 2504.16552 preprint, April 2025 copy at resources/DTVM_paper.pdf). Time to first invocation with lazy JIT on: DTVM 0.95-0.96 ms vs Wasmtime (Cranelift) 20.5-20.6 ms on PolyBench. Table 9 averages: 22.21x over Wasmtime (Cranelift), 4.05x over Wasmer Singlepass, 68.01x over Wasmer Cranelift and 234.13x over Wasmer LLVM on 30 PolyBench cases; on WAPM, 18.87x over Wasmtime, 4.35x over Wasmer Singlepass (one case at 0.49x), 18.66x over Wasmer Cranelift and 197.99x over Wasmer LLVM. Figure 9 shows 21.35x and 21.54x (deriche, doitgen) and 24.51x and 23.36x (echo, pi), so 21.54x is the larger of two displayed PolyBench cases, not a per-case maximum. From the appendix tables (derived from page data): per-case Wasmtime ratios run 19.2-26.0x on PolyBench and 3.2-24.2x on the 20 WAPM packages, and the Wasmer Cranelift PolyBench average is about 22.2x rather than Table 9's 68.01x. Processing time (load + compile + execute; section 5.2.2 says lazy compilation was off): DTVM beats Wasmtime (Cranelift) in 20 of 30 PolyBench cases (1.20x average there, best 1.63x on deriche) and loses the other 10 (0.76x average, worst about 0.57x on trisolv, derived from page data); it averages 11.03-12.14x over the three Wasmer backends. Fibonacci(30): 11.73 ms, which is 11.8% less than Wasmtime (Cranelift) and 25.6%, 29.6% and 40.5% less than Wasmer Cranelift, Singlepass and LLVM. Integer Overflow: 5.5 ms, about 20.6% less than Wasmtime (Cranelift) and up to 64.6% less than the Wasmer variants. The abstract also claims up to 2x over evmone on ERC20/721/1155; that was not checked here.
corrections.workload: PolyBench/C 4.2.1 (30 kernels, int data, DUMP_ARRAYS; the package build notes say SMALL_DATASET) run as archived prebuilt wasm, 20 WAPM packages (time to first invocation only), a recursive Fibonacci(30) and an Integer Overflow (Uniswap-like swap) contract with host APIs mocked in memory. DTVM multipass and lazy JIT are compared against Wasmtime (Cranelift) and Wasmer Singlepass, Cranelift and LLVM.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: PolyBench wasm: archived prebuilt binaries whose toolchain was inferred from binary traces (WASI clang 11.0.0 for 27 cases, 14.0.3 for 3). benchmarks/paper/benchmarks/polybenchc/build.sh reconstructs them with wasi-sdk clang -O3 -DSMALL_DATASET -DDATA_TYPE_IS_INT -DPOLYBENCH_DUMP_ARRAYS -D_WASI_EMULATED_PROCESS_CLOCKS. Paper-era DTVM: commit 882c83155 with LLVM 15. The package's Release build line (-DZEN_ENABLE_SINGLEPASS_JIT=ON -DZEN_ENABLE_MULTIPASS_JIT=ON -DZEN_ENABLE_CHECKED_ARITHMETIC=ON) and run flags (-m multipass [--enable-multipass-lazy] --disable-multipass-greedyra --disable-multipass-multithread) are reconstructions marked 'inferred from xlsx', and the paper does not record its build type. Baselines in the paper text: Wasmtime 31.0.0 (Cranelift) and Wasmer 5.0.5. The package records Wasmer 5.0.4 with Singlepass from v5.0.5-rc1, and its current pins are Wasmtime 45.0.0, Wasmer 7.1.0 (LLVM 21) and DTVM c3c3fd856.
corrections.hardware: Cloud VM, 8 vCPU, 16 GiB, Intel Xeon Platinum 8369B @ 2.70GHz, CentOS 7.9, Linux 3.10.0 (paper section 5). benchmarks/paper/ENVIRONMENT.md records Turbo Boost off only for the contract microbenchmark machine and says the other baselines may have run on a different machine.
corrections.caveats: The paper is a first-party arXiv preprint (arXiv 2504.16552; a v2 exists but arxiv.org is blocked here) by Ant Digital Technologies authors and is not peer reviewed. The reproduction package (benchmarks/paper, added 2026-09) ships cases, version pins and reconstructed scripts but no result data, no per-runtime logs and not the paper's 'Average time' timing script; the contract microbenchmark runner is not included. Its runtimes/dtvm/BUILD.md marks the paper-era DTVM run flags as 'inferred from xlsx'. Its docs/XLSX_FORMAT.md is an issue log: the archived table's cell semantics (compile vs total, ms vs s) are unconfirmed, and the paper's DTVM PolyBench values (2mm 3283.6 ms) match the archived 'dtvm multipass + lazy' total cell (3283.55), although section 5.2.2 says lazy compilation was disabled for that comparison (the eager 'dtvm multipass' cell is 3314.16). The time-to-first-invocation (TTFI) metric is asymmetric. DTVM lazy counts load, lazy precompile, instantiation and the first function's JIT; Wasmtime counts an eager whole-module compile_module(); Wasmer counts Module::new. The package FAQ says DTVM's own eager multipass compile reads about 90 ms on the current build, so the 22x comes from lazy vs eager compilation, not from a faster compiler. Wasmer's three backends post nearly identical processing times about 10x Wasmtime's on compute-heavy kernels (2mm: Cranelift 43.5 s, LLVM 43.9 s, Singlepass 53.0 s vs Wasmtime 3.8 s). LLVM no faster than Cranelift points to a harness or configuration effect in the Wasmer runs, so the 11-12x averages over Wasmer are unexplained. The paper's tables disagree internally. Table 9 lists 30 WAPM cases where appendix Table 12 has 20. Table 9's 68.01x Wasmer Cranelift TTFI average does not match the appendix (about 22.2x, derived from page data). Table 8's Wasmer backend labels are permuted relative to the appendix columns. The build notes say SMALL_DATASET, but the multi-second processing times (2mm 3.3 s) are far above what SMALL_DATASET kernels need, so the dataset size of the archived wasm is unclear. The package's WAPM set replaces the paper's zuk with fortune. zuk was DTVM's worst case: 0.49x vs Wasmer Singlepass and only 3.2x vs Wasmtime. Versions: the paper used Wasmtime 31.0.0 and Wasmer 5.0.x with DTVM 882c83155. The package now pins Wasmtime 45.0.0, Wasmer 7.1.0 and DTVM c3c3fd856 (2026-05-29) for a revised experiment set whose numbers are not in the repo. The package says it is not recorded whether the paper's wall-clock runs cleared the Wasmtime and Wasmer module caches; TTFI runs need WASMTIME_CACHE=0. The README build examples use CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug, which the package warns is far slower than the paper's Release build. Lazy JIT is x86-64 only. The LICENSE is Apache-2.0, with LLVM-derived portions under Apache-2.0 and BSD-3-Clause.

notes: This is a real Wasm VM, and the numbers quoted do appear in the repo's paper PDF. The TTFI headline is lazy-vs-eager compilation (DTVM's eager compile is slower than Wasmtime's per the package FAQ), and processing time beats Wasmtime in only 20 of 30 PolyBench cases at a 1.20x average. Wasmer results look anomalous (all three backends about 10x slower than Wasmtime with LLVM = Cranelift), and the paper's tables have internal inconsistencies (WAPM case count, 68.01x average, lazy-vs-eager column). The repo's own reproduction notes say paper-era flags were inferred, so the tier drops from A to C. Metadata checked: Apache-2.0, 157 stars, last commit 2026-10-08, not a fork. No earlier wave lists DTVM.
